variants.headline: Allies answer the pact against {{opponent}}
body: Our war against {{opponent}} is no longer ours alone. We have been joined by {{allies}}, called to our side by the pact between us, and what one nation carried now rests on several.

variants.headline: More banners against {{opponent}}
body: The coalition against {{opponent}} has grown: our side now includes {{allies}}. A wider war spreads an enemy thin, and every front they must guard is a front where fewer of our men are needed.

variants.headline: Friends keep their word
body: Word from the chancelleries is that the pact has been answered, and our side in the war against {{opponent}} now includes {{allies}}. Treaties honored in hard years are the ones worth signing in calm ones.

variants.headline: Hear it! We do not fight alone
body: News from the war against {{opponent}}: the pact has been honored, and the strength of {{allies}} stands with us. We do not fight alone. Tell it in every street!

variants.headline: Barbarians at the gates of {{cityName}}
body: Scouts report {{barbarians}} barbarians in the country around {{cityName}}. The garrison has been warned; the walls and the herds are both being watched.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Barbarians are at the gates
body: The scouts count {{barbarians}} barbarians outside the walls. Bar the gates, mind the herds, and keep the children close!

variants.headline: The fields around {{cityName}} go quiet
body: The herdsmen saw them first and came in without the herds. {{barbarians}} barbarians now camp within reach of {{cityName}}, and nobody walks the evening roads.

variants.headline: Counting the raiders at {{cityName}}
body: The count near {{cityName}} is not rumor: {{barbarians}} barbarians stand in the surrounding country. A band that size can burn fields and carry off herds faster than a militia can pursue, and the men needed to root it out are men the harvest cannot spare.

variants.headline: The garrison of {{cityName}} stands at {{posture}}
body: It is set down in the record that {{barbarians}} barbarians were counted in the territory of {{cityName}}, and that the command there has answered with a {{posture}} posture.

variants.headline: {{city}} is besieged and starving
body: Enemy forces have closed the roads into {{city}}. No grain is moving in, the granaries are running down, and the city is going hungry.

variants.headline: Who answers for {{city}}?
body: A city under siege eats what it stores and then what it can find, and {{city}} has reached the second stage. The government owes the city a relief plan and a date, and it owes them in that order.

variants.headline: Bread lines in {{city}}
body: Citizens of {{city}}, the siege has reached the table. The baker on the high street opens late and closes early, and the queue starts before his shutters do. No one needs to be told what an empty shelf means.

variants.headline: A call to {{city}} in its hunger
body: The city is besieged and hungry. Keep the gates shut and the shrines open. Feed the poor where you can, and hold to one another. The trial is shared, and so must the bread be.

variants.headline: Heavy damage to {{cityName}}
body: The recent fighting has left {{cityName}} at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}} hit points. Half or more of its defenses are gone.

variants.headline: The state of {{cityName}}
body: City: {{cityName}}.
Defenses: {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}} hit points.
Condition: heavily damaged in the recent fighting.

variants.headline: Abroad tonight, heavy damage at {{cityName}}
body: Abroad tonight. The city of {{cityName}} has taken heavy damage. Its defenses stand at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}} hit points.

variants.headline: The walls of a rival come down
body: {{cityName}}, held by {{civilization}}, stands at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}} hit points. Walls that far gone no longer protect what lies behind them; they only mark where the prize is.

variants.headline: Our forces attack before {{cityName}}
body: Our command before {{cityName}}, a city of {{civilization}}, has gone over to the offensive. The new posture reads {{posture}}.

variants.headline: From {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}
body: The front before {{cityName}} has moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. A change of posture is not a change of mood; it is a conclusion reached by officers paid to reach conclusions. The conclusion says the opening is worth the cost.

variants.headline: The record notes the offensive at {{cityName}}
body: It is set down that our command before {{cityName}}, a city held by {{civilization}}, has taken the posture {{posture}}.

variants.headline: The war moves toward {{civilization}}'s streets
body: The push at {{cityName}} has begun in earnest; the command there has set an offensive posture. Wars are dear to finish, and the last mile of one is always paid in somebody's street.

variants.headline: Our forces return to the fight near {{cityName}}
body: After a withdrawal, the command near {{cityName}} has taken up a new stance against {{civilization}}: {{posture}}. The front there is active again.

variants.headline: The pullback ends at {{cityName}}
body: Our forces had fallen back from {{cityName}}. The new posture, {{posture}}, ends that, and a withdrawal that ends was a repositioning. The ground given up is now ground to retake.

variants.headline: Our forces are back in position near {{cityName}}
body: Near {{cityName}} tonight, our forces are back at the line. The command has moved from withdrawal to {{posture}}.

variants.headline: The second try at {{cityName}}
body: The orders came down, and our men are walking forward again near {{cityName}}. A war that needs two tries at the same ground spends two armies' worth of boots and bread. The council should say what the first withdrawal bought.

variants.headline: Our forces pull back from {{cityName}}
body: Our command before {{cityName}}, a city of {{civilization}}, has shifted from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The units on that front are drawing back.

variants.headline: The withdrawal before {{cityName}}
body: The front before {{cityName}} has gone from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. What the record shows is the change of stance; what it does not show is who ordered it, or what the ground given up was meant to buy. The country can be told both.

variants.headline: Letters from the front: {{cityName}}
body: Letters from the front relate that our forces before {{cityName}} have gone from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The news reached the printer with the evening post, and he passes it on as it came.

variants.headline: The boys are coming back from {{cityName}}
body: Word came ahead of them: our men are off the front at {{cityName}}. Some houses will set a place at the table again. Others will ask, quietly, what the push there cost.

variants.headline: Enemy troops sighted near {{cityName}}
body: Soldiers flying the colors of {{enemies}} have been counted near {{cityName}}. We are at war with them, and they are within reach of the walls.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! The enemy is near
body: Troops of {{enemies}} are sighted outside the walls. Stand to your posts, keep the watch, and leave the roads clear for the army.

variants.headline: What the sighting at {{cityName}} means
body: Troops of {{enemies}} within reach of {{cityName}} can besiege the city, burn its fields, or simply pin its garrison in place. Which of the three comes next will depend on their strength rather than their intentions, and their strength is the number our command should be counting.

variants.headline: Enemy troops just showed up near {{cityName}}
body: The list: {{enemies}}. All of them are at war with us, and all of them are this close.

variants.headline: {{count}} enemy units destroyed
body: Our forces destroyed {{count}} units in the recent fighting, every one of them belonging to the same enemy power.

variants.headline: The enemy's losses, counted
body: Enemy units destroyed by our forces: {{count}}.
All from one enemy army.
Period: the recent fighting.

variants.headline: {{count}} enemy units destroyed in the fighting
body: Our forces destroyed {{count}} enemy units in the latest fighting. All of them belonged to a single enemy army.

variants.headline: Hear it! {{count}} enemy units destroyed
body: The tally from the front is plain: {{count}} of the enemy's units destroyed by our arms. Let the count be told in every street!

variants.headline: A capital falls abroad
body: A foreign capital has fallen by conquest, {{distance}} tiles from our nearest city. The fighting never approached our borders, but the map has been redrawn all the same.

variants.when: cityName !== null && loser !== null && winner !== null
variants.headline: A capital changes hands: {{cityName}}
body: {{cityName}}, the capital of {{loser}}, has fallen to {{winner}} by conquest. A capital is more than a city: whoever holds it holds the machinery of the state. {{winner}} now holds both.

variants.headline: The fall of a capital
body: It is set down that {{winner}} has taken the capital of {{loser}} by force of arms, {{distance}} tiles from our own cities. Providence writes long chapters, and this one is not finished.

variants.headline: Abroad tonight, a capital has fallen
body: Abroad tonight, a capital has fallen to {{winner}}. The city lies {{distance}} tiles from our frontier.

variants.headline: Peace near our borders
body: {{initiator}} and {{target}} have ended their war. The nearer of the two sits {{nearest}} tiles from our border, and the guns between them have gone quiet.

variants.headline: Neighbors at peace again
body: Word reaches us that {{initiator}} and {{target}} have laid down their arms. The peace, concluded near our frontier, asked no visible price of either side. Quiet borders make good neighbors, and ours are quieter this week.

variants.headline: The peace between {{initiator}} and {{target}}
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has ended with no concessions on the record and no capitulation. A peace without terms usually means both sides had spent what they meant to spend. Two neighbors have stopped paying for a quarrel, and the savings are theirs to count.

variants.headline: When the neighbors' fire burns low
body: When the neighbors' fire burns low, your own roof rests easier. So it is with {{initiator}} and {{target}} at peace.

variants.headline: War breaks out near our borders
body: {{initiator}} has opened a war against {{target}}. The nearer of the two sits {{nearest}} tiles from our nearest city, and the war is not ours.

variants.headline: A war next door
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has opened within {{nearest}} tiles of our border, and no war that close is a spectator's affair. Armies forage where they stand, borders close to trade, and both sides will soon be counting what our friendship is worth.

variants.headline: War abroad tonight
body: Abroad tonight: {{initiator}} has attacked {{target}}. The front lies as close as {{nearest}} tiles from our cities.

variants.headline: Their war, our doorstep
body: {{initiator}} and {{target}} are at war, {{nearest}} tiles from our farms. When the great quarrel this close, it is the neighbor's fence that gets trampled first. The council should say plainly what we mean to do about it.

variants.headline: The record of a war nearby
body: It is set down that {{initiator}} made war upon {{target}}, and that the nearer of the two lies {{nearest}} tiles from our lands. The record takes no side; it notes the distance.

variants.headline: A capital falls close to home
body: {{winner}} has taken a capital from {{loser}} by conquest, close enough to our border to be our concern. The map at our doorstep has changed overnight.

variants.headline: What {{winner}}'s capture means here
body: A conquered capital makes {{winner}} a stronger presence on our border and {{loser}} a lesser one. A change of that size, this close, becomes our business whatever flag flies on the walls.

variants.headline: The fall of a capital near our borders
body: In this season {{winner}} took the capital of {{loser}} by the sword. The news came swiftly, for it fell near our marches.

variants.headline: A capital just fell near us
body: {{winner}} has taken a capital from {{loser}}, and not far from us. Here is who got stronger today: not us.

variants.headline: A town changes hands near our border
body: A foreign town has changed hands by conquest {{distance}} tiles from our nearest city. Its old master is not us, and neither is its new one.

variants.when: cityName !== null && loser !== null && winner !== null
variants.headline: {{cityName}} falls to {{winner}}
body: {{cityName}}, lately belonging to {{loser}}, has been taken by {{winner}}. The town lies {{distance}} tiles from our nearest city, and its fields, roads and tolls now answer to another flag.

variants.headline: Notice from abroad: {{cityName}}
body: Notice to travelers and merchants: {{cityName}}, {{distance}} tiles from our cities, has passed to {{winner}} by conquest. Expect a new authority at the gate, and papers to match.

variants.headline: A new flag {{distance}} tiles out
body: {{winner}} has taken a town from {{loser}}, {{distance}} tiles from our nearest city. Whoever holds it now, our border towns will be the first to meet them across the fence.

variants.headline: {{neighbor}}'s army now outranks ours
body: {{neighbor}} now fields a stronger army than we do. The balance between our two nations has tipped, and it did not tip our way.

variants.headline: The tally of arms
body: Their strength: {{theirStrength}}.
Our strength: {{ourStrength}}.
The comparison: theirs is now the larger.

variants.headline: Ask why {{neighbor}}'s army passed ours
body: {{neighbor}}'s army has passed ours in strength. Some counselor will say numbers do not matter. They matter to anyone who shares a border with {{neighbor}}, and we do. The government should account for the gap while it is a gap, not a margin.

variants.headline: The record notes a shift in arms
body: It is recorded that the host of {{neighbor}} has grown past our own in strength. The seasons turn, and the balance of arms turns with them.

variants.headline: Our army passes {{neighbor}}'s
body: Our army has grown past that of {{neighbor}}. The balance between our nations now leans our way.

variants.headline: Our arms in good order
body: The strength of our army now surpasses that of {{neighbor}}, and the credit belongs to those who kept the ranks paid and the armories filled. The nation may take satisfaction in a policy that has borne visible fruit.

variants.headline: Our army just passed {{neighbor}}'s
body: The balance with {{neighbor}} has flipped our way. Strength invites options, and the window for pressing our interests is open.

variants.headline: The account of strength
body: Our strength: {{ourStrength}}.
Their strength: {{theirStrength}}.
The comparison: ours is now the larger.

variants.headline: {{city}} takes heavy damage
body: The recent fighting has taken a heavy toll on the defenses of {{city}}. The walls stand at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}} hit points.

variants.headline: The cost to {{city}}
body: The defenses of {{city}} are down to {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}} hit points. Damage on that scale does not fall from the sky; it gets through when a garrison is thin or relief is late. The city is owed the truth about which one it was.

variants.headline: The crack in {{city}}'s wall
body: The mason came down his ladder at noon and did not go back up. The wall he was repointing stands at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}} hit points, and by evening everyone in {{city}} knew the number.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{city}}! The walls are hurt
body: The enemy has done the walls harm. The defenses stand at {{hitPoints}} of {{maxHitPoints}} hit points. Keep the watch, and mend what is broken.

variants.headline: Our forces counterattack at {{cityName}}
body: Our command at {{cityName}} has shifted from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The front there has passed from holding the line to hitting back.

variants.headline: From defense to the strike at {{cityName}}
body: Our command at {{cityName}} has traded {{previousPosture}} for {{posture}}. A defense that turns to the attack says the enemy has spent his push. The question that follows is whether we have the strength to spend on the answer.

variants.headline: Our forces attack at {{cityName}}
body: At {{cityName}} tonight, our forces have gone over to the attack. The command reports the shift from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}.

variants.headline: The defense holds and answers
body: Advices from {{cityName}} agree that the command there, having held fast through its {{previousPosture}} posture, has now taken the offensive with {{posture}}. The conduct of the front is judged sound, and the judgment is earned.

variants.headline: The front at {{cityName}} goes defensive
body: Our command at {{cityName}} has shifted from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. The front there has settled into defense.

variants.headline: At {{cityName}}, a stance change unexplained
body: Accounts from {{cityName}} agree that our command there has moved from {{previousPosture}} to {{posture}}. No reasons have been given, and this paper can find no one authorized to offer any.

variants.headline: Hear it, {{cityName}}! Our soldiers stand at the walls
body: The command has set a defensive posture around the city. Keep calm, keep the watch, and give the soldiers the road.

variants.headline: The record of {{cityName}}'s front
body: It is recorded that our forces at {{cityName}} took the posture {{posture}}, having before stood at {{previousPosture}}. The change is set down without comment.

variants.headline: A war ends in capitulation
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has ended in capitulation. One of the two now answers to the other. Which of them bows will be plain enough in the seasons ahead.

variants.headline: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} is ended
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} began with calls to arms and closed with a signature and a kneel. The fighting is over. What remains is the peace a victor allows, and a victor's peace is a hard one.

variants.headline: Our war with {{initiator}} ends in capitulation
body: The war {{initiator}} brought to us has closed in capitulation. One of the two nations now rules the other; which way the ruling runs will be plain soon enough.

variants.headline: Our war with {{target}} is settled
body: The peace we concluded with {{target}} is sealed, and sealed with a capitulation. A hard peace, this paper grants, but even a hard peace spares both nations the further cost of the sword. For that much there is reason to be glad.

variants.headline: A peace with visible terms
body: A peace settlement has been recorded, and this one shows its terms: {{count}} concessions, namely {{concessions}}.

variants.headline: The terms between {{initiator}} and {{target}}
body: Peace between {{initiator}} and {{target}}.
Concessions recorded: {{count}}.
The terms: {{concessions}}.

variants.headline: Our peace with {{target}} and its price
body: Our settlement with {{target}} carries {{count}} concessions on the record: {{concessions}}. Which side pays which is nowhere written down, and the government has volunteered nothing. It should.

variants.headline: A peace with terms tonight
body: {{initiator}} and {{target}} have settled their war. The peace carries {{count}} concessions on the record.

variants.headline: Peace on one front only
body: We have made peace with {{settled}}. The war is not over: we remain at war with {{remaining}}, and the guns on those fronts have not stopped.

variants.headline: One account closes, others stay open
body: The settlement with {{settled}} closes one account and leaves the others open. The wars against {{remaining}} continue, and an army freed from one front is only a gain if it is moved to another. Idle strength does not win wars; transferred strength does.

variants.headline: Peace with {{settled}}
body: Peace has been concluded with {{settled}}, and the guns on that front are quiet. This paper notes with regret that the war with {{remaining}} goes on, and hopes the same good sense will find it soon.

variants.headline: Peace for some fronts, marching for the rest
body: The war with {{settled}} is over. The war with {{remaining}} is not. The men already in the field will not come home; they will be marched to a different fire. The council owes the families a count of what is left.

variants.headline: We are at peace
body: No power stands at war with us today. The fighting that filled these pages has stopped, and the country can begin counting what it spent.

variants.headline: The record of rest
body: In this season the fighting ceased, and the nation lay at rest from its enemies. The shrines filled, and the record gives thanks.

variants.headline: The long walk home
body: The roads filled with uniforms walking the other way, and nobody asked for speeches. Quiet is the news now, and the market square knew it before the printer did.

variants.headline: Peace, and what to do with it
body: The fighting is over, and this paper is glad of it. The work it leaves is plain: settle the accounts of the war, care for the people who fought it, and keep the friends we mean to keep. Peace is a season for building, not only for celebrating.

variants.headline: {{count}} of our units lost in action
body: Our forces lost {{count}} units in the recent fighting, every one of them to the same enemy power.

variants.headline: Our losses, counted
body: Our units destroyed in the recent fighting: {{count}}.
All destroyed by one and the same enemy.
The tally is public; the reply is not.

variants.headline: The empty bunks
body: {{count}} units gone in the recent fighting, all to the same enemy. The bunks were stripped before this paper's ink was dry, and the town knew the number before we printed it.

variants.headline: The count from the fighting
body: It is told that {{count}} of our units fell in the recent fighting, and all of them to one enemy. The tellers agree on the number.

variants.headline: Vassals drawn into the war
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} has drawn in vassal arms. The names on the record are {{vassals}}.

variants.headline: What the vassals add
body: Vassals have entered the war between {{initiator}} and {{target}}: {{vassals}}. A vassal's army is not its own to withhold. The master's war becomes the vassal's war, and the list of those fighting is now longer than the list of those with a cause.

variants.headline: The record of vassalage honored
body: It is recorded that {{vassals}} entered the war between {{initiator}} and {{target}}, bound by vassalage. Their banners follow where the master's points, as such banners have always done.

variants.headline: Small kings, big wars
body: The war of {{initiator}} and {{target}} now includes {{vassals}}, who were not asked their view and are not paid to have one. When the great quarrel, the small bleed. Citizens, note how these things are arranged, and by whom.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} stalls
body: Our war with {{opponent}} has lost its motion. The advantage we held has stopped growing, and a war that stops moving keeps costing what it did without gaining what it should.

variants.headline: The stalled advance against {{opponent}}
body: The advantage over {{opponent}} that these pages reported has stopped moving. A stall is not a defeat, but neither is it free: men and stores keep flowing to a front that has stopped returning ground. A war should be measured by what it buys, and this one has stopped buying.

variants.byline: A farmer with a son in the ranks
variants.headline: The war that stands still
body: Madam, the war with {{opponent}} has stopped where it stood, and my son's regiment with it. A war that neither advances nor ends goes on eating its ration of men and money. Will some counselor explain what the standing still is for?

variants.headline: Stuck: the war with {{opponent}}
body: The advantage we were told about has not moved lately. Wars do not pause; they keep costing the same and return less.

variants.headline: Two friends go to war
body: {{first}} and {{second}} have gone to war with each other. Both are friends of ours, and each friendship stands on its own; nothing in either one obliged them to keep the peace with each other.

variants.headline: When friends fight
body: The war between {{first}} and {{second}} puts our two friendships to a test neither was made for. Trade with both and arm neither, and both will call it a slight. Neutrality between friends is a policy with no friends in it.

variants.headline: A plea in the war of {{first}} and {{second}}
body: {{first}} and {{second}} have taken up arms against each other, and both are friends of ours. This paper's wish is plain: that our good offices be offered to both, and that the quarrel end at a table while both sides still have chairs to sit on.

variants.headline: They say the table is broken
body: It is told in the evenings that {{first}} and {{second}}, whose envoys drank from the same cup under our roof, have drawn swords on each other. Old ties, they say, snap loudest.

variants.headline: The war runs long
body: The war has now run {{turns}} turns, past the mark where a war stops being a season's quarrel. From here on, it will be measured less by its causes than by what it eats.

variants.headline: The long stretch of the war with {{opponent}}
body: The war with {{opponent}} has run {{turns}} turns. Duration is itself a fact: armies age, treasuries thin, and the aims a war began with are quietly renegotiated by every season it survives.

variants.headline: The record of a long war
body: The chronicle sets it down: the war has stood {{turns}} turns. Wars of this length were once the business of grandfathers.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} is {{turns}} turns old
body: The war with {{opponent}} is {{turns}} turns old, and nobody remembers what the first week of it was about. The households that waved the first goodbyes have stopped counting weeks.

variants.headline: The nation is at war
body: The nation has entered a new war. The call to arms has gone out, and these pages will follow the fighting turn by turn, wherever it runs.

variants.headline: {{initiator}} has attacked
body: War tonight. {{initiator}} has declared war on us. Our forces are standing to their posts, and the reserves are being counted.

variants.headline: Hear it! {{initiator}} makes war on us
body: Word from the frontier: {{initiator}} has declared war on us. To arms, and mind the stores!

variants.headline: A state of war with {{target}}
body: A state of war now exists between the nation and {{target}}. The government has made its decision, and this paper presumes the decision was not made lightly. It expects the case to be laid before the people before the armies are far from home.

variants.when: role === 'joined' && reason === 'pact' && initiator !== null && target !== null
variants.headline: Their quarrel, our treaty
body: The war between {{initiator}} and {{target}} is now ours by treaty. Pacts are signed in calm years and honored in hard ones; that is their worth and their price. The people should hear from the government what we get for the paying of it.

variants.headline: War on {{count}} fronts
body: The nation is at war with {{enemies}}. The fighting is no longer one quarrel but several, and every front draws on the same purse and the same recruits.

variants.headline: Count the fronts
body: The nation is at war on {{count}} fronts, against {{enemies}}. Every soldier sent to one is a soldier the others go without. The government has yet to say which front it means to win, and a nation that means to win them all wins none.

variants.headline: Hear it! The nation fights on {{count}} fronts
body: The roll of our enemies: {{enemies}}! The war is wide. Keep the fields tended and the watch set.

variants.headline: We are at war with {{count}} powers now
body: The list of enemies: {{enemies}}. Your bread, your sons, your taxes. All {{count}} fronts bill the same house.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} turns against us
body: The war with {{opponent}} has turned. The score stands at {{score}}, deep on their side of the ledger, and the advantage now belongs to them.

variants.headline: The score nobody mentions
body: The war score against {{opponent}} stands at {{score}}. A number that far below even is not bad luck; it is a description of how the fighting has gone. The country can bear the truth, and the government owes it one.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} tonight
body: The recorded score stands at {{score}} in their favor. The balance of the fighting is theirs.

variants.headline: The record of a hard season
body: The chronicle records the war score at {{score}} against us in the war with {{opponent}}. Our fathers knew such seasons. The record preserves them, and does not flatter them.

variants.headline: The war with {{opponent}} turns our way
body: The war score against {{opponent}} stands at {{score}} in our favor. The fighting, of late, has been giving more than it takes.

variants.headline: Reading the war score
body: The score against {{opponent}} has reached {{score}}. A lead of that size is earned in the field, but wars are not won on the ledger; they end when the other side decides the price is beyond paying. The number says we can begin asking.

variants.headline: The war proceeds favorably
body: The war with {{opponent}} proceeds favorably, the score standing at {{score}}. The nation's councils may take satisfaction in the conduct of its arms, and this paper takes some in the saying of it.

variants.headline: Good news, and the bill beside it
body: The war with {{opponent}} is going our way, and the score says so: {{score}}. Good news at last, and the price of it has not left the table.

variants.headline: War weariness eases
body: War weariness across the nation has fallen to {{weariness}}, back below the halfway mark. The mood of the country has lightened with it.

variants.headline: Weariness eases in the war with {{opponent}}
body: Weariness in the war with {{opponent}} has eased to {{weariness}}. The country breathes more easily, and a patient nation makes a better peacemaker than a bitter one.

variants.headline: The number behind the mood
body: War weariness in the war with {{opponent}} is down to {{weariness}}, from above the halfway mark. Weariness does not win wars, but it can lose them. The patience we have just regained is worth more than a battle, because it keeps the country willing to pay for the next one.

variants.headline: War weariness is down to {{weariness}}
body: The country is breathing again. After the long grind, the weariness figure has dropped below half, and you can hear it in the streets.

variants.headline: War weariness sets in
body: The war with {{opponent}} has begun to grind the nation down. War weariness stands at {{weariness}}, past the halfway mark.

variants.headline: A weary nation, and no statement
body: Weariness with the war against {{opponent}} stands at {{weariness}}, past the halfway mark. The council has offered no statement on what the number is to be answered with, and the silence is itself a statement.

variants.headline: Tired of the war? Say it plainly
body: The war with {{opponent}} has run long enough that the country's patience is being measured, and the measure is {{weariness}}. That number is a verdict forming. The council should read it before it hardens.

variants.headline: The record of a weary nation
body: It is recorded that the nation's weariness with the war against {{opponent}} stands at {{weariness}}. Long wars weary the patient.
